paragraphs: The following assessments concern how postsecondary mathematics teachers teach and conduct research. They do not predict hiring, professional titles, qualifications, or appointments.

Postsecondary mathematics teachers focus on teaching and continually improving mathematics and statistics courses: teaching topics such as linear algebra, differential equations, and discrete mathematics; preparing and administering examinations; grading student assignments and papers; preparing syllabi, assignments, handouts, and other materials; planning and revising course content and teaching methods; holding regular office hours to help students; leading classroom discussions; following advances in mathematics and technology; collaborating with colleagues on teaching and research issues; advising students and participating in departmental affairs; and potentially conducting research, publishing findings, and applying for funding.

Entirely fictional task package: Provide a fictional syllabus and student learning data, including 1 set of course objectives and prerequisites, 1 set of assignment and quiz results, and 1 mathematical topic students commonly get wrong. Within 60 minutes, write a lesson plan and explanation approach, an assessment and feedback plan, areas needing tutoring or adjustment, and limitations. Do not use real institution, student, or academic administration data.

Sample output and reflection: Check whether you first defined course objectives and prerequisites, explained assessment definitions, provided actionable explanation and feedback plans, and clarified tutoring and adjustment boundaries. Then ask whether you can sustain lesson preparation and grading, patiently explain material to students with different foundations, and take responsibility for teaching effectiveness and academic standards.

Occupation 25-1022.00 on this page covers mathematical science teachers in higher education who teach mathematics, statistics, and actuarial courses, including teaching-focused and combined teaching and research roles. It excludes primary and secondary mathematics teachers. Lesson preparation, lecturing, test preparation and grading, tutoring, course revision, research, and service vary by position. Do not assume all teachers hold research-focused tenure-track positions; verify appointment requirements for adjacent disciplines separately.

entries: Work inputs: Course objectives and prerequisites, syllabi and textbooks, assignments and examinations, learning and grade data, disciplinary literature and technical advances, student tutoring needs, departmental and committee affairs, and research materials and funding information.

Verifiable outputs: Lesson plans and handouts, syllabi and assignments, examination and grading records, grade and attendance records, tutoring and feedback records, course revision proposals, research papers and reports, funding applications, and service materials.

Complete workflow: Define course objectives and prerequisites → design the syllabus and teaching materials → teach and organize discussion → assign and grade coursework and examinations → provide feedback and tutoring and adjust teaching → revise courses and evaluate effectiveness → conduct research and provide service.

paragraphs: Key judgments: Whether course objectives and assessment definitions are clear, assignments and examinations align with objectives, grading is fair and consistent, differences in students' foundations are addressed, and teaching content and academic practices remain within authorization and disciplinary boundaries.

Environment and pace: Mainly controlled indoor classrooms and offices, with daily email, frequent face-to-face discussions, and public lecturing. Precision matters, decision-making freedom is relatively high, and schedules are generally regular. Most work more than 40 hours a week, including preparation and grading.

Research inputs: Occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 25-1022.00. Wage, employment, and industry data on that page cover this occupation. Research findings are not used to infer mainland Chinese qualifications, pay, or employment definitions.

Check first: Course objectives and prerequisites, assessment definitions and grading criteria, textbooks and teaching resources, student learning and tutoring needs, academic standards and appointment requirements, and research funding and collaboration boundaries.

Work cycle: Start by defining course objectives and prerequisites, then design syllabi and materials, teach and discuss, assign and grade, provide feedback and tutoring, adjust teaching, revise courses, and evaluate effectiveness. Do not grade before confirming assessment definitions and grading criteria, or publish or recommend before clarifying academic standards issues.

Boundaries with adjacent roles: This page covers only postsecondary mathematics teachers. Postsecondary computer science, biological science, atmospheric, earth, marine, and space science, chemistry, and physics teachers teach and research their respective disciplines. Their subject content and appointment requirements are not interchangeable with those on this page.

Postsecondary computer science teachers teach computing and information systems courses; postsecondary mathematics teachers teach mathematics and statistics, with different disciplinary content and methods.

Postsecondary biological science teachers teach biology and conduct biological research; postsecondary mathematics teachers teach mathematics and statistics, with different research objects and methods.

Postsecondary atmospheric, earth, marine, and space science teachers teach earth science courses; postsecondary mathematics teachers teach mathematics and statistics, with different disciplinary foundations.

Postsecondary chemistry teachers teach chemistry and conduct chemical research; postsecondary mathematics teachers teach mathematics and statistics, with different experimental and theoretical methods.
Boundaries of AI impact on postsecondary mathematics teachers

Editorial task hypothesis: Symbolic computation, numerical algorithms, and rule-based grading are separate from generative AI. The latter may draft fictional handouts, exercises, or feedback; occupation-specific adoption rates or job outcomes have not been obtained. Teachers must verify theorem conditions, proof steps, counterexamples, and answers. Numerical output does not prove a proposition. Do not automate final grades; check authorization and applicable privacy rules before disclosing actual student records. AI Impact Score 50% is an editorial estimate. Occupational sources describe actual tasks and objects of work: courses and textbooks, assignments and examinations, learning and grades, and research and service. Tool capabilities, institutional adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately. Wage or employment data are not substitutes for AI evidence.

Editorial comparison: Drafting may be assisted, but no research establishing adoption sequence was obtained. Computer algebra or grading systems do not prove generative AI adoption; teachers must verify grading disputes and proof correctness.

Human control points: Define course objectives and assessment criteria, judge grades and academic standards, design teaching and feedback, take responsibility for student learning and research integrity, and follow institutional and academic ethics requirements.

First conduct an offline exercise using an entirely fictional syllabus and student learning data. Write a teaching and assessment plan without relying on unverified automated grading or generated content to replace teaching judgment.
Editorial hypothesis: Teaching drafts may be assisted; institutional adoption or replacement has not been demonstrated. Symbolic computation differs from generative text.

First verify mathematical conditions, reasoning, and answers, then review against published grading criteria. Do not upload student identities or grades without authorization. Check institutional policies on citations and tool disclosure.

U.S. pay and employment scope for postsecondary mathematics teachers (occupation 25-1022.00)

The 2025 U.S. median annual wage for 25-1022 was $79,940; see the table for all percentiles. No official hourly wage is provided, and none is calculated from annual pay. Older figures of 58,900 employed in 2024 and 4,400 average annual openings in 2024–2034 are listed separately. Latest figures are 57,100 employed in 2025, 2% growth in 2025–2035, and 3,900 average annual openings. These do not represent all postsecondary teachers or individual hiring outcomes.

P10/25/50/75/90 indicate annual wage distribution positions, not beginner or senior levels or take-home income. Full-time or part-time status, contracts, and institutional conditions require separate checks.

Insufficient evidence: Precise industry wages for 25-1022 were not obtained. Reference median annual wages for all postsecondary teaching disciplines in BLS May 2025: state colleges and universities, $96,120; private colleges and universities, $89,660; local junior colleges, $81,640; state junior colleges, $68,160. These include different disciplines and are not industry-specific mathematics teacher wages or employment shares.

The older 4,400 figure is average annual openings in 2024–2034, not a period total. The new 2025–2035 annual average of 3,900 includes replacement openings, distinct from net growth of 1,000 or the annual average of 103,300 for all postsecondary teachers.
Fit signals: Start with observable work behaviors

To assess fit, consider whether you can clearly explain abstract mathematics and design effective practice, patiently work with students with differing foundations, grade rigorously and uphold academic standards, sustain preparation and self-study, and continually improve teaching. Tools such as RIASEC only generate hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.

Positive signals: Clearly explaining abstract concepts, designing practice and assessment, patiently tutoring students, treating grades and standards rigorously, and continually learning and improving.

Reasons for caution: Difficulty explaining abstract material clearly, unwillingness to sustain preparation and grading, a tendency to relax grading criteria or ignore academic standards, or dislike of public teaching and office-hour questions.
Trial action: Using an entirely fictional syllabus and student learning data, practice developing a teaching and assessment plan, then ask someone to review it against your records.

The O*NET interest code is SIC (Social–Investigative–Conventional): an inclination toward teaching and helping others, research and analysis, and organizing information according to procedures. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications.

General personality measures such as the Big Five provide no job-specific evidence for this occupation and support self-reflection only. Continue checking through actual lesson preparation, teaching, grading, tutoring, and research experience.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and support self-reflection only.

Entry pathways and capability stages

O*NET's survey of new hires reports 43% master's degrees, 37% doctorates, and 10% postdoctoral training, not uniform education requirements. Extensive preparation in JobZone5 describes the group. BLS states that four-year institutions typically require doctorates for postsecondary teachers, while community colleges or some part-time positions may accept master's degrees or doctoral candidates. Check specific mathematics positions and institutions; do not impose a fixed requirement for years of prior teaching.

In the U.S., mathematics or related master's or doctoral education plus teaching assistant or teaching and research practice; verify education requirements by institution type. Articles 2 and 4 of China's Regulations on Teacher Qualifications require those specializing in education and teaching to obtain teacher qualifications by law, including higher education teacher qualifications. Separately verify degrees, examinations, and qualification recognition; recognition does not equal a university appointment or professional title. Check current local recognition materials and institutional position requirements separately.

Degrees, teacher qualifications, and professional titles are different statuses. Completing a degree or obtaining teacher qualifications does not automatically confer an appointment or title. Check conclusions about teaching qualifications, title evaluation, and research integrity against responsible authority and institutional rules.

Entry stage: Under supervision, practice lesson preparation and teaching, grading and feedback, office-hour tutoring, and teaching material production. Learn academic standards and institutional requirements and retain teaching and assistantship records.

Evidence to show: Use verifiable teaching materials and a feedback explanation, including course objectives, teaching design and assessment methods, and student feedback or grade analysis, to demonstrate teaching design and honest documentation.

Next step: Check the target institution's course and teaching requirements, education and appointment conditions, and research and publication requirements. Verify teaching, assessment, and tutoring abilities in supervised real teaching.

Progression to greater responsibility: With experience, lead core courses and curricula, mentor and advise students, develop teaching and research expertise, or move into departmental administration, research, or education.
Market signals and transition directions

Older figures of 58,900 employed in 2024 and 4,400 average annual openings in 2024–2034 are retained. Latest figures are 57,100 employed in 2025, 2% growth in 2025–2035, and 3,900 average annual openings. Projections include full-time and part-time work and do not equal secure full-time or tenured positions. Check specific contracts and institutional budgets.
The main industry on that page for 2024 is Educational Services. Employment and openings are statistical projections and must be interpreted separately from individual opportunities.

Transferable capabilities: Mathematics and statistics knowledge, teaching design and delivery, assessment and feedback, academic writing and research, data analysis and modeling, advising, communication, and collaboration.

First target, postsecondary computer science teacher: Build disciplinary depth for programming, data structures, and software design courses, laboratory and project assessment, and corresponding research or teaching appointment evidence. Mathematics and statistics teaching and general grading skills transfer, but deeper mathematics or a shift toward data science does not cover all gaps for this target.

source_card.note: Source scope, limitations, and statistical periods are checked separately against original evidence. Source use notes: O*NET 25-1022.00 Mathematical Science Teachers, Postsecondary (Summary): Provides occupational identity, official description, interest code, Job Zone, skills, and knowledge for 25-1022.00.; Wage and employment data on that page cover this occupation.; Hourly wages are not displayed on that page.; O*NET 25-1022.00 Tasks: Provides a task list including teaching linear algebra and differential equations, preparing and administering examinations, grading and recordkeeping, preparing course materials and syllabi, revising courses, providing office-hour tutoring, leading classroom discussions, and conducting and publishing research.; The task sample does not mean every position performs every task.; O*NET 25-1022.00 Work Context: Describes mainly controlled indoor settings, daily email and face-to-face discussions, frequent public lecturing, relatively high decision-making freedom, and an emphasis on precision.; U.S. work context does not replace Chinese law or institutional procedures.; O*NET 25-1022.00 National Wages (BLS OEWS display): Median annual wage from 2025 BLS OEWS; the page covers this occupation.; Hourly and percentile wages are not displayed on that page.; O*NET 25-1022.00 National Employment Trends: Employment size in 2024, growth in 2024–2034 (slower than average at 1%–2%), and projected job openings.; Projections are not hiring guarantees.; Industries: 25-1022.00: The main industry on that page for 2024 is Educational Services.; Industry distribution signals employer settings, not projected growth or demand.; O*NET 25-1022.00 Education and Career Preparation: Job Zone 5: Most positions require graduate education (about 43% master's, 37% doctoral, and 10% postdoctoral training).; The education distribution does not constitute mandatory requirements for every employer.; Licenses & Certifications: 25-1022.00: State licensing and national certification search tools provided by O*NET.; Certification and training do not equal appointment eligibility or employer hiring requirements.; Generative AI and Jobs (ILO Working Paper 140, 2025): Assesses occupational exposure to generative AI at the task level.; The exposure index does not equal adoption rates, job outcomes, or hiring probabilities.; Average Annual Wages of Persons Employed in Urban Units in 2025: Provides average annual wages by broad industry category for urban non-private and private units, including education.; An industry average is not an occupational median and excludes individual businesses and freelancers.; FermatMind Postsecondary Mathematics Teachers Task Impact Scale: Organizes tasks that can be assisted and human control points for task-level discussions of AI and fit.; This editorial scale is not evidence of adoption rates, layoffs, regulations, or licensing.;

description.text: Mathematics teachers on this page refers to O*NET 25-1022.00: teaching linear algebra, differential equations, and discrete mathematics; preparing and administering examinations; grading and recording grades; preparing course materials and syllabi; revising content; providing office-hour tutoring; leading classroom discussions; following disciplinary developments; and conducting and publishing research. To assess this career path, verify the work cycle, responsibility and evidence boundaries, evidence definitions, risk controls, and observable entry-level work samples together.
